families.decision: Organic or grass-fed whole milk, not ultra-pasteurized, cream-top when sold.
buying_tips: Look for the USDA Organic seal or the AGA 100% Grassfed logo on the carton.
Read the carton for “ultra-pasteurized” and pick one without it.
Pick non-homogenized or cream-top milk when the case carries it.
Skip lowfat, skim and flavored milk; pick plain whole milk.

families.decision: Plain whole-milk organic cultured dairy with live cultures and no thickeners.
buying_tips: Read the label for named cultures or “contains live and active cultures”.
Skip tubs listing pectin, gums, starch or carrageenan as thickeners.
Pick plain and check that Added Sugars reads 0g on the panel.
Look for the USDA Organic seal or the AGA 100% Grassfed logo on the tub.

families.decision: Organic or grass-fed block cheese of milk, cultures, salt and rennet.
buying_tips: Read the front name and skip “cheese food”, “cheese product” and spreads.
Check the list for sodium citrate or other emulsifying salts and skip them.
Pick a block or wedge over individually wrapped slices.
Look for the USDA Organic seal or the AGA 100% Grassfed logo on the label.

families.decision: Organic or grass-fed butter, cream and ghee with nothing added but salt.
buying_tips: Read the butter list: cream, and salt if salted, nothing else.
Skip whipped butter and spreads that blend butter with vegetable oils.
Check cream cartons for “ultra-pasteurized” and added gums or emulsifiers.
Look for the AGA 100% Grassfed logo or the USDA Organic seal on the pack.

families.decision: Organic unsweetened plant milk of the named plant and water, no oils or gums.
buying_tips: Read the list: the named nut, grain or bean and water, little else.
Pick “unsweetened” and check that Added Sugars reads 0g.
Skip cartons listing vegetable oil, carrageenan or gums.
Look for the USDA Organic seal and a printed plant percentage.

families.decision: Organic full-fat coconut milk listing only coconut and water.
buying_tips: Read the list for coconut and water only, no guar gum or thickeners.
Skip cans labeled light or low-fat; they are diluted with water.
Look for “BPA-free lining” on the can, or pick an aseptic carton.
Look for the USDA Organic seal on the can or carton.

families.decision: Organic ice cream of cream, milk, sugar and egg yolks, without gums.
buying_tips: Read the front name for “ice cream” or “frozen custard”.
Skip tubs listing guar gum, carrageenan or other stabilizers.
Pick a pint that feels heavy for its size, since whipped-in air weighs little.
Look for the USDA Organic seal or the AGA 100% Grassfed logo on the carton.

families.decision: Organic live ferments labeled unpasteurized, kept cold, short ingredient list.
buying_tips: Look for an organic seal and fermented or live-cultures wording on the jar or bottle.
Read unpasteurized, raw or not heated after fermentation on the label.
Check the cold case, keep-refrigerated wording, the date and an intact seal.
Pick short recipes of named whole foods, salt and cultures.

aisles.decision: Plain, whole, organic or grass-fed dairy first; plant milks with the shortest list.
buying_tips: Look for the USDA Organic seal or the AGA 100% Grassfed logo on each pack.
Read each ingredient list and pick the shortest one with nothing added.
Check milk and cream for “ultra-pasteurized” and pick the carton without it.
Ask staff whether the store sells raw milk, where state law allows it.

whole_vs_reduced_fat_milk.short_answer: Pick plain organic or grass-fed whole milk without “ultra-pasteurized” on the carton. Cream-top or non-homogenized milk is the next step up when the case has it.
pick_steps: 100% grass-fed on milk means the cows ate grass and hay, never grain.
Read the carton for “ultra-pasteurized” and skip it.
Look for “low-temperature” or “vat pasteurized” printed on the label.

raw_milk.decision: Cream-top grass-fed milk; raw only where stores sell it.
raw_milk.delta: Raw milk is sold in stores in only a few states, labeled raw on the bottle.
raw_milk.short_answer: Most stores sell no raw milk. The closest shelf option is organic or grass-fed whole milk, low-temperature pasteurized and non-homogenized. Where a store does sell raw milk, the bottle says raw.
pick_steps: Look for “vat pasteurized” or “low-temperature” on the bottle.
Pick non-homogenized, cream-top milk with an AGA Grassfed seal.
Ask staff whether the store sells raw milk, where state law allows.

goat_sheep_dairy.decision: Plain whole goat or sheep milk first, then organic.
pick_steps: Read the ingredients for goat milk or sheep milk.
For sheep milk cheese, look for feta, pecorino romano, Roquefort or Manchego.
Look for USDA Organic: certified organic feed and outdoor access.
goat_sheep_dairy.cart_pick: Plain whole goat or sheep milk
buying_tips: The animal on the list decides the food; goat butter, for one, comes out white.
Look for goat or sheep milk, cultures and salt alone on a cheese or yogurt list.
Read the ingredients for goat milk or sheep milk.
Look for feta, pecorino romano, Roquefort or Manchego for sheep milk cheese.
Expect goat butter to be white, not yellow.
Homogenized or ultra-pasteurized: see Milk.

cheese_real_vs_processed.decision: Grass-fed block cheese first, then organic; never cheese food.
pick_steps: Read the front name: ‘cheese product’, ‘cheese food’ or ‘process’ means emulsifiers.
Look for USDA Organic: certified organic feed and outdoor access.
Buy the block; bagged shreds carry starch, cellulose and natamycin.
buying_tips: Bagged shreds are coated in starch to keep them apart, which is why they melt poorly.
Look for 100% grass-fed milk named on the block.
Look for a short list: milk, salt, cultures, enzymes/rennet.
Raw-milk cheese from grass-fed herds is the top rung. Imported and deli-counter wheels are the easiest raw finds.
Skip cheese made from homogenized milk.
Smoked cheese should be smoked over real smoke, not liquid smoke or smoke flavoring.
‘Parmesan’ is a generic word in the US. ‘Parmigiano-Reggiano’ is a protected one with a stamped rind.
Keep hard-cheese rinds. They belong in a pot of beans or soup.
The milk for cheese may come from cows given the synthetic growth hormone rBST. Certified organic rules exclude its use.

Certified organic block cheese is the first choice. Next, find a wrapper stating the cheese uses milk from cows given no rBST. Cheese with neither claim is last. US labeling does not require a statement about rBST use.
“rBST free” on a wrapper points to milk from cows not given rBST.

pick_steps: Read the rind label for “raw milk” or “lait cru” and an age.
Ask the cheese counter whether the wedge was aged 60 days or more.
Start with hard, aged styles: alpine, aged cheddar, manchego, pecorino.

grassfed_butter.decision: Grass-fed butter of cream and salt first, then organic.
grassfed_butter.delta: Butter must be at least 80 percent milkfat, made from milk or cream alone.
pick_steps: Skip tubs and spreads; butter comes as a block or a stick.
Look for USDA Organic: certified organic feed and outdoor access.
Look for the AGA Grassfed logo on the wrapper.
grassfed_butter.cart_pick: Grass-fed butter, cream and salt only

pick_steps: Read the milkfat: heavy cream is 36% or more, half-and-half 10.5 to 18%.
Read the list too: even real cream can carry carrageenan or gellan gum.
Skip a creamer whose list opens on water, sugar and oil.
For plain ghee, pick a jar listing butter alone.
Skip jars listing natural flavors.
Look for the AGA 100% Grassfed logo or USDA Organic seal.

oat_milk.short_answer: Pick organic unsweetened oat milk listing oats and water, with no added oil or gums. Check that the Added Sugars line reads 0g, barista versions included.
pick_steps: Read the list for oats and water first.
Skip cartons listing sunflower, canola, rapeseed or other oils.
Skip cartons listing gellan, guar or locust bean gum.
Pick unsweetened over sweetened, vanilla or chocolate.
Skip cartons listing sunflower, safflower, canola or other oils.

raw_kefir.decision: Plain whole-milk kefir first, then organic or raw where sold.
pick_steps: Take it from the refrigerated case; shelf-stable kefir’s cultures are no longer live.
Read the label for live and active cultures named on the bottle.
Look for USDA Organic: certified organic feed and outdoor access.
